children.text: Business Platform – Multi-Tenant Business Management Platform

The Business Platform is a full-stack application designed to give businesses direct control over the information displayed on their websites while allowing developers to focus on building and maintaining the websites themselves.

Businesses frequently need to make small changes such as updating menu items, prices, hours, contact information, social media profiles, or images. Normally, these changes require the business to contact a developer each time something needs to be updated. The Business Platform creates a shared workspace where authorized business users can manage this information themselves and custom client websites can retrieve the latest data through the platform's API.
Each business can have its own custom-built website with a unique design, branding, domain, and page structure while still using the same shared backend infrastructure.
The platform is built around three main pieces:
Handles authentication, accounts, workspaces, dashboards, business management, API routes, and database access
Provides the interface used by owners, administrators, staff, and developers
Can be designed independently for each business
Retrieve only the data belonging to their associated business
Connect to the shared platform using a Business API Key
Business and location identifiers are used to keep records separated
Supports multiple businesses and multiple locations within the same platform
This allows client websites to remain visually independent while sharing the same content-management infrastructure.
The platform provides tools for managing the information commonly required by business websites.
The dashboard includes create, update, delete, reorder, validation, loading, empty, success, and error workflows for managing business content.
The application is divided into several areas based on the type of information being managed.
Users can manage information related to their own account.
The workspace provides business-level management features such as:
The dashboard focuses on the content that appears on client websites.
This separation keeps account, business administration, and website content management organized into their own workflows.
Google authentication is supported as the initial sign-in provider, allowing authenticated users to access their account, businesses, and authorized platform features.
Protected server routes validate the user's session and business access before allowing business data to be viewed or modified.
Users are connected to businesses through business memberships rather than having one global role.
This means one account can belong to multiple businesses and have a different role within each one.
The platform currently supports the following access levels:
Can create, update, and delete business content
Can manage general user information with restrictions around ownership
Does not have permission to modify business content
Handles the technical connection between the platform and client websites
Can only manage Business API Keys
This permission model separates business management responsibilities from developer responsibilities while allowing the same platform to support different types of users.
A user account can be connected to more than one business.
Instead of storing a single business role directly on the user, the platform uses a business membership relationship that connects:
The role belongs to that specific membership.
This allows scenarios such as the same user being:
Businesses can contain one or more physical locations.
Business content is organized at the location level so different locations can be maintain independent:
This allows a business with multiple locations to represent differences between those locations while still managing everything through one business workspace.
The platform also supports synchronization of records across business locations.
Records can belong to synchronization groups so the same information can be maintained across several locations.
Synchronization can be used with information such as:
A business can choose whether a record should remain synchronized or become unique to a specific location.
This provides flexibility for businesses where most information is shared across locations but certain products, hours, or other information differ.
The platform contains a hierarchical menu system.
A location can contain categories, and categories can contain both:
Menu items can also contain additional options.
Categories, items, and item options contain ordering information so businesses can control how their menu is presented rather than relying on creation order.
All items contain information such as:
Each location contains its own weekly schedule.
This allows each location to maintain independent operating hours while still supporting synchronization when several locations share the same schedule.
Custom client websites retrieve business information through the Business Platform API.
Developers can generate Business API Keys through the business workspace.
An API key identifies which business is requesting data so a client website receives only the dataset associated with that business.
The complete key is only exposed when it is generated. A short key prefix can remain visible afterward for identification without displaying the original secret.
The generated key can then be stored in the client website's environment configuration.
The platform does not force every business website to use the same frontend. Instead, developers are free to build a completely custom client website based on the needs of the business.
One business might use a restaurant-style website while another could use an entirely different design and page structure.
Both can retrieve their data from the same platform.
The first client website used with the platform is Tacos El Guero (a previous client of mine). Development has not yet started as I am still working through some fixes.
The application uses PostgreSQL with Prisma for its data layer.
The database was designed around several primary relationships:
Business-owned and location-owned relationships help prevent data from one tenant from being mixed with another.
Database constraints and indexes are also used to maintain consistency for values such as:
Slugs are system-generated URL-safe identifiers used for stable routing and data retrieval.
The platform generates slugs using rules such as:
Business slugs are globally unique, while item slugs are scoped to their associated data.
Slugs are generally kept read-only so changes made by business users do not unexpectedly break URLs, data fetching, or image references.
Business images are stored using a private Amazon S3 bucket.
Clients never receive AWS credentials and do not communicate directly with S3.
Instead, image operations follow a backend-controlled flow:
Frontend → Next.js Route Handler → Authentication / Business Validation → Image Validation → Image Processing → S3 Helper → Amazon S3
The database stores an S3 object key instead of a permanent public image URL.
The object key remains stable even when an image is replaced.
When access to an image is required, the backend can generate a temporary presigned URL instead of exposing the bucket or permanent object location.
Uploaded images are processed before being stored.
Sharp is used to generate an optimized WebP version of supported images.
The application compares the processed WebP image against the original upload and stores whichever version is smaller.
This reduces unnecessary storage and bandwidth without requiring business users to manually optimize their images before uploading them.
The platform validates information before it reaches the database.
Validation is used throughout forms and server requests to help prevent malformed or invalid data from being stored.
The project uses tools including Zod and React Hook Form for validation and form-management workflows.
Automated testing covers both backend and frontend behavior.
External dependencies such as Prisma, authentication, S3 operations, and image-processing boundaries can be mocked so tests do not communicate with production services.

Type safety across the frontend, backend, forms, and database access

Backend, API, validation, and utility testing
Designed and built a multi-location business platform with Google sign-in, account onboarding, business creation and joining, and role-based access
Developed cross-location content syncing while preserving each location's independent data and settings
Designed a PostgreSQL data model for multi-location businesses, including hierarchical menus and rules that keep related data consistent
Built backend APIs in TypeScript with Next.js Route Handlers, using Prisma and PostgreSQL to manage business data and serve client websites through an API key
Implemented secure S3-based image management with backend-controlled uploads, stable object keys, image processing, and temporary media access
Built comprehensive workspace and dashboard interfaces for managing users, menus, items, contacts, socials, locations, and operating hours
Implemented automated testing across API behavior, authentication, authorization, validation, image management, and frontend interactions
Wrote architecture documentation to guide development and maintain consistency across the frontend, backend, database, storage, and client integration

Tacos El Guero is a responsive restaurant website built for a local food business. The project was developed by working directly with the restaurant owners to understand what they wanted from their website, translate those requirements into features, and refine the application through feedback before launch.

The website was built using React and Vite and deployed to AWS using S3 and CloudFront. The project focused on creating a simple and accessible online presence for the business while making restaurant information easy for customers to find and navigate.
The website provides a customer-facing experience for discovering information about Tacos El Guero.
The application was designed around the needs of the restaurant and its customers, with an emphasis on:
Responsive layouts across desktop and mobile devices
A design tailored to the restaurant's branding and needs
This project was developed directly with the restaurant owners rather than from a predefined set of project requirements.
Translating business needs into website features
Designing and implementing the user interface
Iterating on the website based on owner feedback
Preparing and launching the finished website
This process allowed the website to evolve based on feedback from the people who would actually be using it to represent their business.
The interface was designed to remain responsive across different screen sizes so customers can access the website from both desktop and mobile devices.
The production website is hosted using AWS.
Hosts the application's static production files
Stores the compiled website generated by the Vite build process
Distributes the website through AWS's content delivery network
Serves the deployed application to users
After production updates, new builds can be uploaded to S3 and CloudFront cache invalidations can be performed when necessary so visitors receive the latest version of the website.

Akkadian is an AI-assisted syllabus builder designed to help instructors create and organize course syllabi through a structured, evidence-based workflow. The application breaks the syllabus creation process into multiple sections so instructors can progressively build course information, learning objectives, assessments, materials, and policies within one interface.

The application was built with Django and HTMX, allowing individual sections of the interface to update dynamically without requiring full page reloads. TailwindCSS and DaisyUI were used to build responsive and reusable interface components, while PostgreSQL was used to store course and syllabus information.
This project was developed as a university capstone by a 7-person Agile development team.
The syllabus builder separates course creation into multiple interactive sections:
Allows instructors to enter and manage general course information
Supports course descriptions and learning objectives
Helps organize assessments and align them with course objectives
Provides additional tools for reviewing and refining assessment information
Allows instructors to manage materials associated with the course
Provides an interface for adding and managing syllabus policies
Each section is designed as part of a larger workflow so instructors can progressively build their syllabus instead of managing all course information within a single large form.
HTMX is used throughout the application to provide dynamic interactions while keeping Django responsible for server-side rendering.
Instead of refreshing an entire page when course information changes, the application can request and replace individual sections of the interface.
This approach was used for features such as:
Submitting forms without full page reloads
Updating related interface components after changes
Reusable Django templates and partials are used to keep these workflows consistent throughout the application.
The interface was designed to provide a consistent experience across the different syllabus-building modules.
Responsive and reusable UI components were created so similar controls, layouts, forms, and interactions could be shared across multiple sections of the application.
Django is used for the application's backend and server-side rendering.
PostgreSQL is used to store application data related to courses, syllabus content, assessments, materials, policies, and other course information.
The frontend communicates with Django primarily through normal requests and HTMX requests.
Akkadian was developed by a 7-person Agile team as a capstone project.

This is a VUI (Voice User Interface) that assist users with food products. The app works like a VA where there are three intents and 15 utterances in each one. Through voice commands, the application detects which intent it belongs to and outputs the desired outcome for that intent. This app is meant to assist users choosing the right, and healthier, food product, and it can also serve as a nutrition app where the user can ask to compare two products to see which one is healthier.

This is a full-stack analytics dashboard that allows users to explore and visualize data from the videogame industry. The application uses the Steam and IGDB APIs to retrieve videogame information and displays the data through interactive charts, filters, and responsive components.

The dashboard is meant to make large amounts of videogame data easier to understand by presenting the information visually and allowing users to filter and explore different parts of the videogame market.

The frontend was built with React and Vite, while an ExpressJS backend handles requests to the external APIs and delivers processed data to the frontend. ChartJS is used for data visualizations, and Vitest is used to test API response processing and application functionality.
The application is deployed and can be accessed through the hosted frontend
Displays videogame data, filters, and ChartJS visualizations
Handles requests to the Steam and IGDB APIs
Processes API responses before returning data to the frontend
Filtering systems for exploring different datasets
Server-side processing of external API responses
The application retrieves videogame data from two external APIs:
Provides information related to games available through Steam
Requests are handled through the ExpressJS backend
Provides additional videogame and industry information
API responses are processed by the backend before being sent to the frontend

The React frontend does not communicate directly with these external APIs. Instead, requests are sent to the ExpressJS backend hosted on Render, which communicates with the external services and returns the required data to the frontend.
ChartJS is used to transform retrieved videogame data into interactive visualizations.
Users can use filtering options throughout the dashboard to change which data is displayed and explore different areas of the videogame market.
The visualizations make the API data easier to read and understand than viewing the raw API responses directly.

The application uses separate deployments for the frontend and backend.

files.what: I build apps that actually solve real-world problems. I take high risk and I'm always committed with the work I'm assigned. Im a builder by heart and always wants to know more about how something is built (technical or not).
files.when: Im always programming every day; learning to use a new stack or continuing my work on a personal project. You can check out what im currently working on by running the command "cd ~/projects/personal"!
files.where: I was born in California Orange County and then moved to Portland Oregon at the age of 4. Fun fact: in middle school I started to grow a liking in my art classes to where I started drawing in a journal of what ended up becoming pages of a game I created where I drew the playing field and characters that can be used with all of their stats and other info. I never wanted to become a game developer but it eventually made me lean into game development where I learned the classic Scratch, into eventually Unity. Ive uploaded the games I've created in my personal projects directory if you'd like to view them :)
files.who: A 2026 Portland State University Alumni who focuses on Frontend Technologies where React, Next.js, PostgresSQL, and TypeScript have become my preferred and most favorite stacks to work with.
files.why: I love every part of creating a web page, either business or not. The good ol' days of web development is nothing like what it is today, and for a good reason. As difficult as it has gotten, I've never given up on web development and I dont plan too. Creating websites is more than just skill to me but apart of who I am. I admire the beautiful, fluent applications I see online and try to learn from them; trending UI, illustration patterns, and their simple UX. My journey technically begin in 2023 when I took my first intro class to web development, but I am primarily self-taught and have always been eager to learn more.
